question: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?

raiseTranscript.text: I decided to refactor a module without checking the test coverage first. It broke two downstream services and we had to roll back.
What did you do after the rollback?
I wrote a one-page note on what signals I should have checked and shared it with my mentor. On the next change I asked for a quick review before touching shared code.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Chose to refactor without checking coverage; broke two services
Rolled back same day
Quote: "I wrote a one-page note... and asked for a quick review before touching shared code"
Follow-up: Asked what signals were missed; candidate described adding pre-change checklist
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for a junior. The candidate owned a narrow-scope refactor that caused a rollback and then documented the missing signals. The follow-up shows they turned the incident into a repeatable checklist they now use. This matches the expected level of individual ownership plus quick adoption of feedback. Biggest strength is the concrete post-incident action rather than generic learning statements.

lowerTranscript.text: I picked the wrong library because the team lead suggested it. It didn't scale and we had to rewrite the feature.
I would ask more questions next time so someone else catches it earlier.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Blamed library choice on team lead suggestion
Outcome: rewrite required
Quote: "I would ask more questions next time so someone else catches it earlier"
Follow-up: Probe on personal ownership produced only external attribution
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. The candidate attributed the poor library choice to a suggestion from the lead and framed the lesson as asking others to catch issues. No evidence of personal decision process or concrete steps taken afterward. At junior level this shows missing ownership and limited coachability.

raiseTranscript.text: I pushed to launch a new API version across two teams without a staged rollout. Latency spiked for one partner and we lost a day of data.
How did you involve the other team?
I had only sent an email. After the incident I ran a retro with both teams and we added a shared canary requirement for any cross-team API change.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Decided on full launch without staged rollout; affected partner data
Cross-team impact visible
Quote: "After the incident I ran a retro with both teams and we added a shared canary requirement"
Follow-up: How did you involve the other team? Candidate admitted email-only communication and created joint process
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The decision had measurable cross-team impact and the candidate ran a retro that produced a durable process change used by both teams. Shows influence without authority and willingness to surface the mistake publicly. Biggest strength is converting the failure into a shared safeguard rather than an individual fix.

lowerTranscript.text: I approved a vendor contract that later turned out to have hidden fees. The team had to absorb the cost.
What changed in how you review contracts now?
I make sure finance reviews everything first so I don't miss those details again.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Approved vendor contract with hidden fees; cost absorbed by team
No metrics on impact size
Quote: "I make sure finance reviews everything first so I don't miss those details again"
Follow-up: Probe on process change showed delegation to another function only
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. The candidate describes a contract mistake but the only learning is routing everything to finance. No evidence of building judgment for future decisions or raising standards for the broader org. At senior level this lacks cross-team leverage and process ownership.

raiseTranscript.text: I staffed a critical project with a strong but overloaded engineer. Delivery slipped two weeks and the engineer burned out.
How did you handle the underperformance signal?
I met with the engineer weekly, adjusted scope, and later changed our staffing model to include explicit load reviews before every major project.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Overloaded key engineer on critical project; two-week slip and burnout
Team-level outcome affected
Quote: "I later changed our staffing model to include explicit load reviews before every major project"
Follow-up: How did you handle the underperformance signal? Candidate described weekly 1:1s and permanent process change
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The decision produced both delivery and people impact. The candidate adjusted in real time and institutionalized a load review that prevents recurrence across the team. Shows ownership of team outcomes and development of repeatable mechanisms. Biggest strength is the shift from individual recovery to org-level safeguard.

lowerTranscript.text: I promoted someone too early. They struggled and we had to move them back to individual contributor.
What did you change about promotion decisions?
I now wait longer before promoting so I have more data.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Early promotion led to demotion
No team-level process described
Quote: "I now wait longer before promoting so I have more data"
Follow-up: Probe on process change produced only personal caution, no team mechanism
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. The promotion mistake is acknowledged but the only adjustment is personal caution. No evidence of creating leverage for the broader team or addressing underperformance signals systematically. At manager level this misses the expectation of building durable team processes.

raiseTranscript.text: I chose to acquire a small company to accelerate a capability instead of building it. Integration took longer than modeled and we missed a market window by nine months.
What trade-off did you revisit afterward?
We added an explicit build-versus-buy scorecard with integration risk weights and now require two scenarios before any acquisition decision.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Acquisition decision missed market window by nine months
Business-level impact and long-term process change
Quote: "We added an explicit build-versus-buy scorecard with integration risk weights"
Follow-up: What trade-off did you revisit? Candidate described org-wide decision framework
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The decision carried clear business-level ambiguity and long-term cost. The candidate created a reusable scorecard that changed how future strategic choices are framed. Shows strategic judgment and leverage through process rather than heroics. Biggest strength is institutionalizing the lesson at the right level of the organization.

lowerTranscript.text: We entered a new geography too quickly. Revenue came in below plan and we pulled back after 18 months.
What would you change in future market entries?
I would make sure the local team has more runway before we commit capital.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of a time you made a poor decision. What happened and what did you learn?
Geography expansion missed revenue plan; pulled back after 18 months
No org-level mechanism created
Quote: "I would make sure the local team has more runway before we commit capital"
Follow-up: Probe on strategic learning stayed at personal preference
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. The market entry mistake is described but the learning remains an individual preference rather than a structural change. No evidence of strategic trade-off frameworks or long-term organizational judgment. At exec level this lacks the leverage and pattern recognition expected.

diagnostic.manager: Names team outcome and people cost
Staffing model change for whole team

diagnostic.exec: Changes acquisition process for entire org
